## 4 Proofs from the main text in more detail

#### Lemma 2 from the main text.

The following results are true for the infection turnover rate $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ when $\theta(0)$ is sufficiently close to 1:

- 1. $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}>\gamma$ while $\dot{J}(t)\geq 0$ .

- 2. $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}<\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ always, and $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ can be made to stay arbitrarily close to $\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ for an arbitrary amount of time while $\theta(t)\approx 1$ by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1.

- 3. $\lim\limits_{t\to\infty}\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}=\max\left\{\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right),0\right\}$ .

#### Proof.

We begin by establishing that $J(t)$ and $I(t)$ have peaks at times greater than 0. For $J(t)$ , we see from its logarithmic growth rate

$$ \frac{d}{dt}\log J=\frac{\dot{J}}{J}=\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)}{\psi^{\prime}(\theta)}\dot{\theta}+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma) $$

that $J(t)$ is increasing at $t=0$ (since $\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(0))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)\approx(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)>0$ and $\dot{\theta}(0)\approx 0$ ) and that $J(t)$ is decreasing for $t\to\infty$ (since $\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))<\frac{\psi^{\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{1-\theta(\infty)}=\frac{\beta+\gamma}{\beta}\psi^{\prime}(1)$ by the convexity of $\psi^{\prime}$ and $\dot{\theta}<0$ ). Thus, $J(t)$ has a peak time $t_{J}>0$ . And since the peak $t_{J}>0$ of $J(t)$ exists, it is easy to see that the peak $t_{I}>0$ of $I(t)$ will also exist from the fact that $\dot{I}=J-\gamma I$ and that $I$ initially increases (as shown for $\mathcal{R}_{0}>1$ by Miller [41]).

Now to prove the first result, note that $\dot{J}=\ddot{I}+\gamma\dot{I}$ . At the peak of $I(t)$ , $\dot{I}=0$ and $\ddot{I}<0$ , implying $\dot{J}<0$ . It must then be true that at the peak of incidence $J(t)$ , the prevalence $I(t)$ has not yet reached its peak and so $\dot{I}>0$ . Therefore, at and before the peak of incidence, we must have $\frac{J}{I}=\frac{\dot{I}+\gamma I}{I}>\gamma$ .

For the second result, define $\alpha(t)=\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)I(t)-J(t)$ . First we see that $\alpha(0)>0$ , since for $\theta(0)\approx 1$ we have $I(0)=1-\psi(\theta(0))\approx\psi^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))$ and

$$ \displaystyle J(0) \displaystyle=\psi^{\prime}(\theta(0))\left(\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime}(\theta(0))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)(1-\theta(0))\right) \displaystyle\approx\big(\beta\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)-(\beta+\gamma)\psi^{\prime}(1)\big)(1-\theta(0)), $$

so that

$$ \lim_{\theta(0)\to 1}\frac{J(0)}{I(0)}=\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma). $$

Now we can easily derive from $\dot{J}=-\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)\dot{\theta}^{2}+\beta(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1)J-\gamma J$ that

$$ \dot{\alpha}=\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)\dot{\theta}^{2}+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}J-\gamma\alpha, $$

which, in combination with $\alpha(0)>0$ , shows that $\alpha(t)>0$ for all $t$ . This proves the first part of the second result, that $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}<\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ always, assuming $\theta(0)$ is sufficiently close to 1.

The second part of the second result also follows from Eq. (S22). To see this, note that the first two terms of Eq. (S22) both go to 0 as $\theta\to 1$ , so while $\theta(t)\approx 1$ , $\alpha(t)$ tends at rate $\gamma$ to very small quantities (which can be made arbitrarily small for as long as desired by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1). And since $I(t)$ is also increasing while $\theta(1)\approx 1$ , then $\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)-\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}=\frac{\alpha(t)}{I(t)}$ can be made arbitrarily small for arbitrarily long by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1.

For the third result, we can formulate $I(t)$ and $J(t)$ explicitly as

$$ I(t)=e^{-\gamma t}I(0)+\int_{0}^{t}e^{-\gamma(t-s)}J(s)ds $$

and

$$ J(t)=-\psi(\theta(t))\dot{\theta}(0)\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}\left(\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)\right)ds\right) $$

from $\frac{\ddot{\theta}}{\dot{\theta}}=\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma).$ Thus, we can get

$$ \frac{J(t)}{I(t)}=\frac{-\psi(\theta(t))\dot{\theta}(0)\exp\left(\int_{0}^{t}\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)ds\right)}{I(0)-\int_{0}^{t}\psi(\theta(s))\dot{\theta}(0)\exp\left(\int_{0}^{s}\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\tau))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)d\tau\right)ds}. $$

Now let $c=\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ . We consider the behavior as $t\to\infty$ of Eq. (S25) for the cases of $c>0$ , $c<0$ , and $c=0$ . In the first case ( $c>0$ ),

$$ \frac{J(t)}{I(t)}\to\frac{-\psi(\theta(\infty))\dot{\theta}(0)\frac{1}{c}\left(e^{ct}-1\right)}{-\int_{0}^{t}\psi(\theta(\infty))\dot{\theta}(0)\frac{1}{c}\left(e^{cs}-1\right)ds}\to c\text{ as }t\to\infty, $$

as the term encompassed by the outer integral in the denominator of Eq. (S25) for later $t$ will come to dominate that term in the integral for earlier $t$ as well as the constant $I(0)$ . In the second case ( $c<0$ ), the numerator of Eq. (S25) goes to 0 as $t\to\infty$ while the denominator remains at least $I(0)$ , and so $\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}=0$ . In the last case ( $c=0$ ), we first must note that the integral $\int_{0}^{\infty}\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)ds$ will converge since $\theta(s)-\theta(\infty)$ for large $s$ behaves as an exponential decay (see Eq. (S27) below). Thus, for large $t$ , Eq. (S25) will look like $\frac{A}{B+At}$ with $A=-\psi(\theta(\infty))\dot{\theta}(0)\exp\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)ds\right)$ and $B$ some positive constant, showing that $\lim\limits_{t\to 0}\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}=0.$ To complete the proof just requires establishing $\theta(t)-\theta(\infty)$ behaves as an exponential decay for large $t$ . Let $\Theta(t)=\theta(t)-\theta(\infty)$ and then this follows from the following approximation for when $\Theta\approx 0$ :

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\Theta} \displaystyle\approx-\beta(\Theta+\theta(\infty))+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta(\infty))+\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))\Theta}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}+\gamma\big(1-(\Theta+\theta(\infty))\big) \displaystyle=\left(\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)\right)\Theta, $$

where the first approximation follows from the Taylor expansion $\psi^{\prime}(\theta(\infty)+\Theta)\approx\psi^{\prime}(\theta(\infty))+\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))\Theta$ and the second step follows from $\dot{\theta}(\infty)=-\beta\theta(\infty)+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}+\gamma(1-\theta(\infty))=0$ . We remind the reader that $\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta(\infty))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)<0$ , as we showed at the beginning of this proof, to ensure that the behavior of $\Theta(t)$ is in fact an exponential decay for large $t$ . ∎

#### Theorem 3 from the main text.

In the limit as $\theta(0)\approx 1$ , the infected degree distribution $X(t)$ will approach the neighbor degree distribution $K_{\textnormal{n}}$ at some time $t$ . Specifically, for any small $\varepsilon>0$ and $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , there exists a $\theta(0)$ and time $t_{\varepsilon}$ for which $\left\lvert p_{j}(t_{\varepsilon})-\frac{P(k)k}{\mu}\right\rvert<\varepsilon$ for all $j\leq k$ .

#### Proof.

Filling in the gaps from the proof outline in the main text, we first show that the peak time $t_{J}$ of $J(t)$ is greater than 0 and that $\theta_{J}=\theta(t_{J})$ is constant regardless of initial condition. The fact that $t_{J}>0$ we established in our proof here of Lemma 2. To see that $\theta_{J}$ is constant regardless of initial conditions, it suffices to set $\dot{J}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\left(-\psi^{\prime}(\theta(t))\dot{\theta}(t)\right)=0$ , which gives $\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta)\dot{\theta}^{2}+\psi^{\prime}(\theta)\ddot{\theta}=0$ and thus

$$ \frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}\left(-\beta\theta_{J}+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}+\gamma(1-\theta_{J})\right)+\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)=0, $$

from which we see that $\theta_{J}$ is evidently independent of initial conditions.

We now give an explicit choice of $\theta(0)$ and $t_{\varepsilon}$ which ensure, for a given choice of small $\varepsilon>0$ and large $k\in\mathbb{N}$ , that $\left\lvert p_{j}(t_{\varepsilon})-\frac{P(k)k}{\mu}\right\rvert<\varepsilon$ for all $j\leq k$ . First, we repeat the following two equations from the main text for convenience:

$$ \dot{p}_{k}=-\frac{J}{I}\left(p_{k}-\frac{P(k)k\theta^{k}}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log\theta)}\right) $$

and

$$ \theta(t)>1-(1-\theta(0))e^{(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)t}\ \text{ for all }t>0. $$

Now let $\theta_{\varepsilon}$ be a value of $\theta$ close enough to 1 so that

$$ \left\lvert\frac{P(j)j\theta^{j}}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log\theta)}-\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}\right\rvert<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\text{ for all }\theta_{\varepsilon}\leq\theta\leq 1\text{ and }j\leq k. $$

Then choose $t_{\varepsilon}>0$ such that

$$ \displaystyle\left\lvert\left(P(j)-\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}\right)e^{-\gamma t_{\varepsilon}}\right\rvert<\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\text{ for all }j\leq k. $$

We define $t_{\varepsilon}$ this way since Eq. (S29), Lemma 2, and $p_{j}(0)=P(j)$ imply that $p_{j}(t)$ will approach $\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}$ faster than will $\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}+\big(P(j)-\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}\big)e^{-\gamma t}$ while $\theta(t)\approx 1$ . Of course, $p_{j}(t)$ is not actually approaching $\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}$ , but while $\theta(t)\geq\theta_{\varepsilon}$ , it is approaching something that is within $\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ of $\frac{P(j)j}{\mu}$ ; thus, if $\theta(t)\geq\theta_{\varepsilon}$ for all $t\leq t_{\varepsilon}$ , we will have $\left\lvert p_{j}(t_{\varepsilon})-\frac{P(k)k}{\mu}\right\rvert<\varepsilon$ for all $j\leq k$ . In order to ensure $\theta(t)\geq\theta_{\varepsilon}$ for all $t\leq t_{\varepsilon}$ , we simply let $\theta(0)=1-\frac{1-\theta_{\varepsilon}}{e^{(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)t_{\varepsilon}}}$ and then we will have our desired result by Eq. (S30). ∎

#### Theorem 5 from the main text.

If $\theta(0)$ is sufficiently close to 1, then $m(t)$ and $I(t)$ will both peak at times $t_{m}>0$ and $t_{I}>0$ respectively. And as $\theta(0)$ approaches 1 both $t_{m}$ and $t_{I}$ will diverge to $\infty$ while

$$ 0<\lim_{\theta(0)\to 1}\frac{t_{m}}{t_{I}}<\frac{1}{2}-\frac{\gamma}{4(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)+2\gamma}. $$

#### Proof.

Filling in the gaps from the proof outline in the main text, we first show why $\lim\limits_{\theta(0)\to\infty}t_{m}=\infty$ . From Eq. (S30), we see that $\theta(t)$ can be kept arbitrarily close to 1, and thus $\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(\log\theta(t))}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log\theta(t))}$ kept arbitrarily close to $\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(0)}{\varphi^{\prime}(0)}$ , for as long as desired by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1. Then since $\dot{m}=-\frac{J}{I}\left(m-\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(\log\theta)}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log\theta)}\right)$ , $m(t)$ can be made to take arbitrarily long to peak by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1 so that the moving target $\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(\log\theta)}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log\theta)}$ that $m(t)$ tends toward stays sufficiently constant, noting that the rate at which $m(t)$ tends towards this target ( $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ ) is bounded above and below by positive constants by Lemma 2. In order to apply Lemma 2 here to get that $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ is bounded below by $\gamma$ , it must be noted that $\theta(t)\geq\theta_{J}$ (we showed previously that $\theta_{J}$ is a constant regardless of initial condition that satisfies Eq. (S28)) and thus $t\leq t_{J}$ while $\theta(t)$ is kept sufficiently close to 1, as we are assuming is the case here.

Next we prove that $\lim\limits_{\theta(0)\to 1}\frac{t_{I}}{t_{J}}=1$ . We first point out that in our proof of the first result of Lemma 2, we showed that $J(t)$ peaks before $I(t)$ , or $t_{J}<t_{I}$ . In the proof of Lemma 2, we also use Eq. (S23), which shows that as $\theta(0)\to 1$ and $t_{J}\to\infty$ , the behavior of $I(t)$ for after $t_{J}$ will approximate

$$ \displaystyle I(t_{J}+\tau)\approx C+ \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\tau}e^{-\gamma(\tau-s)}\psi^{\prime}(\theta(t_{J}+s))\left(\beta\theta(t_{J}+s)-\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta(t_{J}+s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-\gamma(1-\theta(t_{J}+s))\right)ds $$

for $\tau>0$ , where $C=\int_{0}^{t_{J}}e^{-\gamma(t-s)}\psi^{\prime}(\theta(s))\left(\beta\theta(s)-\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta(s))}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-\gamma(1-\theta(s))\right)$ approaches a constant as $\theta(0)\to 1$ and $t_{J}\to\infty$ due to the deterministic trajectory of $\theta$ . Thus, the time $\tau$ that it takes for $I(t)$ to peak after $J(t)$ peaks, or $t_{I}-t_{J}$ , will approach a constant as $\theta(0)\to 1$ . Then since both $t_{I}$ and $t_{J}$ go to $\infty$ as $\theta(0)\to 1$ , their ratio $\frac{t_{I}}{t_{J}}$ will go to 1.

Next we show $\lambda_{2}=(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)-\frac{\beta}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}\left(\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)-\frac{\psi^{\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{1-\theta_{J}}\right)>0$ . Rearranging this inequality gives

$$ 1-\theta_{J}<\frac{\beta}{\beta+\gamma}\frac{\psi^{\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}, $$

so this is the result we are trying to prove. Now rearranging Eq. (S28), we get

$$ \displaystyle 1-\theta_{J} \displaystyle=\frac{\beta}{\beta+\gamma}+\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}-2\frac{\beta}{\beta+\gamma}\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)} \displaystyle=\frac{\beta}{\beta+\gamma}\frac{\psi^{\prime}(1)-\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-\frac{\psi^{\prime}(\theta_{J})}{(\beta+\gamma)\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}\left(\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)\right), $$

so it just suffices to show that $\beta\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(\theta_{J})}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-(\beta+\gamma)>0$ . This follows from Eq. (S28) because the expression inside the large parentheses there is $\dot{\theta}(t_{J})$ , which is negative by the ever-decreasing nature of $\theta(t).$

Lastly, we give an explicit formula for $t_{m}$ in the limit as $\theta(0)\to 1$ , derived from (27) in the main text, which we reproduce here for convenience:

$$ \lim\limits_{\theta(0)\to 1}\dot{m}(t)=-\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}\left(m-\big(f(1)-f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))e^{(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)t}\big)\right)\text{ for all }t\leq t_{m} $$

converges uniformly across $t\leq t_{m}$ , with $f(x)=\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(\log x)}{\varphi^{\prime}(\log x)}$ . Thus $f(1)=\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(0)}{\varphi^{\prime}(0)}$ and $f^{\prime}(1)=\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}(0)}{\varphi^{\prime}(0)}-\left(\frac{\varphi^{\prime\prime}(0)}{\varphi^{\prime}(0)}\right)^{2}$ . We now treat $\dot{m}(t)$ as being (approximately) equal to its limit from Eq. (S35) and treat $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ as being (approximately) equal to $\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ , since Lemma 2 shows that $\frac{J(t)}{I(t)}$ can be arbitrarily close to $\beta\left(\frac{\psi^{\prime\prime}(1)}{\psi^{\prime}(1)}-1\right)$ for as long as desired while $\theta(t)\approx 1$ by choosing $\theta(0)$ sufficiently close to 1. Doing so gives the (approximate) differential equation

$$ \dot{m}(t)\approx-(\lambda_{1}+\gamma)\left(m-\big(f(1)-f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))e^{\lambda_{1}t}\big)\right) $$

with $\lambda_{1}=(\beta+\gamma)(\mathcal{R}_{0}-1)$ and $m(0)=\mu$ , which has explicit solution

$$ m(t)\approx f(1)-\frac{\lambda_{1}+\gamma}{2\lambda_{1}+\gamma}f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))e^{\lambda_{1}t}-Ce^{-(\lambda_{1}+\gamma)t} $$

with $C=f(1)-\mu-\frac{\lambda_{1}+\gamma}{2\lambda_{1}+\gamma}f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))$ a constant so that $m(0)=\mu$ . To find the peak time $t_{m}$ in this limit, we set Eq. (S36) equal to 0, or equivalently, set

$$ f(1)-\frac{\lambda_{1}+\gamma}{2\lambda_{1}+\gamma}f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))e^{\lambda_{1}t_{m}}-Ce^{-(\lambda_{1}+\gamma)t_{m}}\approx f(1)-f^{\prime}(1)(1-\theta(0))e^{\lambda_{1}t_{m}} $$

which gives

$$ t_{m}\approx\frac{1}{2\lambda_{1}+\gamma}\left(\log\frac{1}{1-\theta(0)}+\log\frac{(2+\frac{\gamma}{\lambda_{1}})C}{f^{\prime}(1)}\right). $$

Again this approximation becomes asymptotically correct as $\theta(0)$ approaches 1. As $\theta(0)\to 1$ , the $\log\frac{1}{1-\theta(0)}$ term will dominate and we get $\lim\limits_{\theta(0)\to 1}\frac{t_{m}}{\log\frac{1}{1-\theta(0)}}=\frac{1}{2\lambda_{1}+\gamma}$ as desired. ∎
